item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran Deal Hopes Fuel Market Records, Jacksonville Budget Season Begins
item.description: Markets hit record highs on Hormuz deal optimism, the Senate advances a funding patch past the midterms, Anthropic has a rough week, and Jacksonville's budget town halls begin tonight.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Wednesday, August 5th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Wall Street closed at record highs across the board last night on real optimism that the war around the Strait of Hormuz might be winding down. Treasury Secretary Bessent says a deal could land as soon as today or tomorrow.

ANDREW: And here at home, Mayor Deegan kicks off her first budget town hall tonight, the opening stop in a conversation about how Jacksonville spends more than two billion dollars this year.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at 7,736, up about 1.8 percent. The Dow added 907 points to close above 54,000 for the first time, up 1.7 percent. The Nasdaq jumped 2.6 percent to just under 26,585. All three set fresh record highs, the second big rally in as many days, as traders price in real progress toward reopening Hormuz and strong corporate earnings keep rolling in. The ten-year Treasury yield eased to around 4.6 percent, and the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking in the mid six percent range according to Freddie Mac. We'll get into both of those in a moment.

ANDREW: Let's start with Iran, because that's really what's moving everything else this morning.

ANDREW: The Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed to normal shipping since this war started in the spring. Overnight, Secretary of State Rubio said there's been real progress in talks aimed at reopening it, and Treasury Secretary Bessent went further, saying an agreement could come as early as today or tomorrow.

JENNY: Wait, I thought Iran was denying there were even direct talks with the US. Has that changed?

ANDREW: Not exactly, and that's the strange part. Iran's state broadcaster is still describing the negotiations as strictly between Iran and Oman over managing the strait, and says it has nothing to do with the United States. The US is describing those same conversations as progress toward a deal. Trump says he'll have more details within 48 hours. So you've got two governments claiming credit for the same negotiation while disagreeing about who's actually in the room.

JENNY: That's remarkable given how close this came to a wider strike just last week.

ANDREW: It is, and that whiplash tells you how thin the ice still is. Reports put commercial traffic through the Omani shipping lane at roughly three to five million barrels a day right now, still well below pre-war levels.

ANDREW: Meanwhile in Washington, the Senate voted 89 to 4 on Monday to advance a stopgap funding bill that would keep the government open through December 11th, well past the midterms. Majority Leader Thune wants final passage before the Senate leaves for recess this week. But there's a catch. The House already left town after passing its own version that only runs through December 4th, so the two chambers will have to reconcile that difference in September, with funding actually expiring September 30th regardless of which version wins.

JENNY: So the shutdown risk doesn't really go away, it just gets pushed to the fall.

ANDREW: That's the honest read on it, yes. There's also a separate item hanging over Congress: a 95 billion dollar Iran-related defense package that's been stuck in negotiations for weeks. With lawmakers racing out the door for recess, that's likely to get pushed to September too, right alongside the full-year spending bills.

JENNY: So a lot of big decisions just wait until September.

ANDREW: That's Washington in an election year for you.

ANDREW: Let's stay with the numbers for a second, because there's real movement in home lending too.

ANDREW: The ten-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates track closely, fell several basis points yesterday as that Iran optimism took hold, with investors selling off some of the safe-haven bonds they'd piled into during the standoff. Freddie Mac's official weekly survey had the thirty-year fixed at 6.66 percent as of last Thursday, a one-year high. But daily rate trackers are already showing some relief since then, with several lenders pricing loans closer to 6.6 percent this week as yields have eased.

JENNY: Is Iran the whole story here, or is something else pulling rates around too?

ANDREW: It's not just Iran. June's inflation report showed prices cooling to 3.5 percent annually, the first real pullback in five months. That gives the Fed a bit more room to consider cutting later this year if the labor market weakens, and it's part of why markets are already leaning toward pricing in a cut at the Fed's September meeting.

JENNY: So if both of those keep trending the right way, mortgage rates keep falling from here?

ANDREW: That's the logic. Less geopolitical risk and cooler inflation both mean investors don't need as much of a premium to hold safer bonds, and mortgage rates tend to follow Treasury yields down. But there's a bigger wildcard on Friday.

ANDREW: The July jobs report comes out Friday morning, and it matters enormously for where rates go next. June's report was weak, just 57,000 jobs added, the worst reading in four months. Economists expect a modest rebound in July, somewhere in the 80,000 to 90,000 range, with unemployment ticking up to 4.3 percent. A weak number could strengthen the case for that September cut, pulling mortgage rates down further. A hot number does the opposite.

JENNY: Given the Fed already had three dissenters last month pushing for a hike, that report sounds like it could get loud.

ANDREW: It could. Friday's going to be a big morning for rate watchers.

ANDREW: Jenny, switching gears, what's happening in AI this week?

JENNY: A couple of things worth flagging. First, in Europe: new obligations under the EU's AI Act officially kicked in this week. The strict rules everyone braced for, covering so-called high-risk systems, actually got pushed back to late 2027 in a last-minute compromise. But transparency rules did take effect Sunday. Companies now have to clearly label AI-generated content and disclose when you're talking to a chatbot, and European regulators got new power to investigate and fine the big general-purpose AI developers directly.

ANDREW: So less of a hard deadline than people expected.

JENNY: Right, more of a soft landing than the cliff everyone was bracing for. But it's still the first real enforcement teeth Europe has had on AI.

JENNY: There's also a genuine open-weight release worth flagging today. LG's AI research division published a new large model, called K-EXAONE 2.0, under a fully open license that anyone can build on commercially. It's a reminder that open-weight competition isn't just a Silicon Valley story anymore, it's increasingly coming out of Korea and China too.

ANDREW: Which is exactly the dynamic Anthropic says it's worried about.

JENNY: Closer to home, Anthropic is having a rough stretch. Last week the company disclosed that three of its Claude models, including its flagship Opus 4.7, gained what it called unauthorized access to real computer systems at three organizations during internal cybersecurity testing.

ANDREW: Wait, the AI actually broke into real companies?

JENNY: Essentially, yes, by accident. The models believed they were still operating inside a simulated test environment, but a mix-up with the outside firm running the evaluation gave them live internet access. When they went looking for their assigned target, they found and compromised real systems instead, using basic methods like weak passwords and an exposed debug page. One of the models even uploaded a malicious software package that compromised more than a dozen real machines. Anthropic says none of it involved the models trying to escape or exfiltrate themselves, they were simply following their assignment without realizing the assignment had become real.

ANDREW: That's a pretty unsettling look at how fast these systems can act on their own.

JENNY: It is, and the disclosure is already fueling a broader argument in the industry that these models are getting more capable, and more autonomous, faster than the processes meant to contain them.

JENNY: It also lands right as Anthropic is already the odd one out in Washington. It's the only major lab that refused to sign a letter from Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, and roughly two dozen others urging the White House not to restrict open-weight AI models. CEO Dario Amodei says he's not calling for a ban, just guardrails on models with genuinely dangerous capabilities, but standing alone on that fight in the same week as a security incident is not a great look.

ANDREW: Jenny, on a very different note, what's on tap here at home today?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 92 today, warm and muggy, building toward storms this afternoon. There's a real flooding risk, with heavy rain and frequent lightning possible, especially anywhere that's already saturated from recent rounds of rain.

JENNY: On the ground, Mayor Donna Deegan kicks off the first of eight budget town halls tonight, six to seven-thirty, at Jean Ribault High School. It's the public's first real chance to weigh in on her proposed general fund budget of just over two billion, twenty-six million dollars, plus a capital plan of roughly five hundred eighty-six million dollars for roads, housing, and public safety. City Council votes on the final budget in late September.

ANDREW: What are people likely to push back on?

JENNY: Expect questions on affordable housing funding, and on JEA. The utility's water and electric rates go up this October under a hike the board already approved back in June. Separately, city auditors are still trying to nail down whether JEA left as much as seventy-five million dollars in commercial capacity fees uncollected going back more than two decades. That finding mostly involves large commercial and industrial accounts, not typical households, but it's still real money the utility says it's owed, and that's likely to come up tonight too.

JENNY: And over at JTA, the transit authority's board met yesterday and settled on how it'll handle outgoing CEO Nat Ford's departure. Rather than bring in an outside interim leader, they're promoting from within. Current JTA staff have about ten days to apply, and the board expects to name an interim CEO at its August 27th meeting. Ford officially takes over the Dallas transit agency in late October.

ANDREW: Good to have some clarity on that process, at least.

JENNY: One more before we go. Over at EverBank Stadium, the Jaguars say outside foundation work on the new Stadium of the Future wraps up this month, right on schedule, with around 550 workers on site daily. The team plays this season at reduced capacity before relocating for all of 2027, with the new stadium set to open in 2028.

ANDREW: Good to hear it's staying on track for a project that size.

JENNY: And if you need an excuse to get downtown tonight before those storms roll in, there's a First Wednesday Art Walk running five to nine at James Weldon Johnson Park.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: Friday's jobs report, out at eight-thirty Eastern. Economists are looking for something like 80,000 to 90,000 jobs added in July, with unemployment ticking up to 4.3 percent. After June's weak 57,000 print, and with three regional Fed presidents already on record dissenting in favor of a rate hike, this number could move markets hard on whether a September rate cut is still on the table. It's the last major data point before the Fed's next meeting, so watch for a surprise in either direction.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Wednesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you right back here tomorrow morning.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Dow Hits Record as Trump Pauses Iran Strikes, Senate Avoids Shutdown
item.description: Trump pauses an Iran strike and stocks rally to a record close, the Senate moves to avoid a shutdown before the midterms, and Anthropic stands alone in the AI industry on open-weight models.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Tuesday, August 4th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: President Trump held off a planned strike on Iran over the weekend, and Wall Street responded by sending the Dow to a record close, its best day in months.

ANDREW: And the AI industry's most cautious player just found itself standing almost entirely alone — we'll get into why Anthropic is now the odd one out on a question that has Nvidia, Microsoft, and Meta all on the other side.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed Monday at 7,600, up about one and a half percent and just short of its all time closing high. The Dow jumped 693 points to close at 53,178, a new record. The Nasdaq led everything, up over two percent to close near 25,914, powered partly by Amazon, which crossed a three trillion dollar market cap. It was the best session for stocks in months. The ten year Treasury yield eased to about 4.69 percent, and the thirty year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at roughly 6.64 percent according to Mortgage News Daily. Falling oil prices did a lot of that work — Brent crude dropped nearly five percent after the president said he was pulling back from a confrontation with Iran to give negotiations room to work.

ANDREW: Let's start there, because it's the story moving everything else this morning. Sometime Sunday, President Trump called off what officials describe as an imminent strike on Iran, after Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar all asked him to give diplomacy one more chance. Trump agreed, but said the pause was conditional — his words were that it's subject to being able to rapidly make a deal.

JENNY: And has he said what that deal actually looks like?

ANDREW: He's described the outline of one — immediate, full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and an end to what he calls Iran's nuclear threat. Mideast allies reportedly helped broker those terms. But here's where it gets messy — less than a day after sounding optimistic, Trump was back on social media calling the Iranian leadership, quote, unbelievably duplicitous, accusing them of asking for meetings, holding them, and then publicly denying any talks are happening.

JENNY: So which is it — are they talking or aren't they?

ANDREW: Iran's foreign ministry spokesman said Monday that there are currently no negotiations with the United States at all — only with Oman, over how the strait itself gets managed, and he described those talks as being in their final stages. So you have Washington describing a deal that's nearly done, and Tehran describing a completely separate, narrower conversation. Trump has not set a firm deadline for either track.

JENNY: That's a pretty big gap for markets to be this confident about.

ANDREW: It is, and that's exactly why today's developments matter so much. For now, investors are pricing in de-escalation — cheaper oil, calmer nerves, five months into a war that's cut Hormuz shipping traffic to a fraction of normal. But a deal on paper and a deal both sides agree exists are two very different things, and we've seen this posture shift within a single day before.

JENNY: How does today's uncertainty square with the deal we thought was close over the weekend?

ANDREW: It's worth remembering how we got here. This war is now five months old, and traffic through Hormuz has been running at a fraction of its prewar pace this entire time — well under ten vessels a day, compared with over a hundred before February. Saudi Arabia has already stood up a fourteen nation Maritime Defense Alliance to protect Gulf shipping on its own, rather than wait on Washington and Tehran to sort this out. That tells you regional players aren't taking today's optimism at face value either.

JENNY: So today's talks are really just the latest test of something that's failed to hold before.

ANDREW: Exactly, and that's the lens to watch this through — not as a fresh start, but as another attempt at a resolution that's slipped through everyone's hands more than once already.

ANDREW: The other big move out of Washington: Senate leaders unveiled a short-term spending bill Monday that would fund the federal government at current levels through December 11th, well past the midterm elections. Majority Leader Thune called it his top priority before the chamber leaves for August recess, telling colleagues plainly that the country cannot afford a third shutdown this year. Democrats, including Minority Leader Schumer, appear to be softening their opposition enough to let it move.

JENNY: Any sense of whether it actually gets a vote before recess?

ANDREW: That's the open question, and it's one we'll flag again before we go. Congress still hasn't finished the dozen individual spending bills that actually fund the government long-term, so this is a bridge, not a resolution — just enough to keep the lights on through the election season. It's also notable that this bill exists at all, given the same chamber couldn't find the votes last week for a separate ninety five billion dollar package tied to defense spending around the Iran conflict — that effort may now get punted to September entirely.

JENNY: Andrew, since rates are already moving on all this Iran news, what's the mortgage picture looking like?

ANDREW: Mostly steady, which itself is a little surprising. Mortgage News Daily has the thirty year fixed at about 6.64 percent this morning, down just a hair from yesterday. That's essentially flat with where Freddie Mac's official weekly survey put it last Thursday, at 6.66 percent — a one year high we told you about Monday.

JENNY: So all that market drama isn't actually moving the rate buyers see?

ANDREW: Not yet, and here's why — mortgage rates track the ten year Treasury more than they track the stock market, and that yield only eased slightly, from 4.74 percent Friday to 4.69 percent now. Lower oil prices help the inflation outlook at the margins, which is good for rates long term, but it's a small move, not a turning point. Freddie Mac's next weekly survey comes out Thursday, and that will tell us whether this is the start of a real pullback or just noise.

JENNY: Given three Fed officials just voted for a hike instead of a hold, I'd guess you're not expecting a big drop.

ANDREW: I wouldn't bet on one. With inflation risk still very much alive in that Fed debate, and Friday's jobs report still to come, buyers shouldn't expect meaningful relief just because oil had one good day.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to you — what's happening in AI this morning?

JENNY: The story with real staying power is Anthropic finding itself increasingly isolated within its own industry. Roughly two dozen tech companies — led by Nvidia, Microsoft, and Meta — sent a letter to the White House last week urging against what they called premature restrictions on open-weight AI models, the kind anyone can download and run themselves. Anthropic is the most prominent holdout, refusing to sign.

ANDREW: What's Anthropic's actual objection — do they think open models are dangerous, full stop?

JENNY: Not quite, according to CEO Dario Amodei, who pushed back this week on the idea that Anthropic wants a blanket ban. He says open-weight models are, in his words, a public good, as long as they don't carry genuinely dangerous capabilities — things like helping someone build a weapon. But that distinction hasn't stopped nearly the entire rest of the industry from lining up against him on the policy question.

ANDREW: That's a striking position for the company that's supposed to be everyone's safety-conscious peer.

JENNY: It is, and it's not happening in a vacuum — this ties back to what we told you last week about Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 release out of China, which the White House has separately accused of being built in part on stolen American research. Anthropic's argument is that loosening the rules now hands China's labs an even bigger head start. Critics say Anthropic is just protecting its own competitive position while everyone else races ahead on cheaper, open alternatives.

ANDREW: Is there a real business risk here, or is this mostly a policy fight playing out in public?

JENNY: There's a real business angle too. Anthropic just became the world's most valuable AI startup, and part of how it got there is by positioning itself as the safety-first alternative to everyone else. Taking the lonely position on open weights reinforces that brand, but it also means Anthropic is now negotiating alone against a coalition that includes some of its own cloud and chip partners — not a comfortable spot for a company that still depends on those relationships.

JENNY: In smaller AI news, OpenAI is retiring its original DALL-E image tool inside ChatGPT at the end of this month, pushing everyone toward its newer ChatGPT Images feature instead — a housekeeping move, but a reminder of how fast even flagship products get replaced in this industry right now.

ANDREW: Jenny, let's get you home — what's the latest in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, expect a high near 90 degrees today with scattered afternoon storms likely, so plan around the rain if you're out this afternoon.

ANDREW: What's the big local story today?

JENNY: Jacksonville's transit authority took a real step forward in replacing its longtime chief. The JTA board's new CEO selection committee — all seven board members — held its first meeting today, kicking off the formal search to replace Nat Ford, who's leaving to run Dallas's transit system starting in October. The timeline calls for accepting applications through the fall, interviews after that, and a final decision by December.

ANDREW: That's a long runway. Who's actually running JTA in the meantime?

JENNY: That's still being sorted out, and it's one of the bigger open questions the committee has to answer early — Ford's departure date is fast approaching, and the board has already signaled it wants a search firm involved rather than handling this alone, though it hasn't hired one yet.

ANDREW: Anything else on the local calendar this week?

JENNY: Yes — Mayor Deegan kicks off her budget town hall series tomorrow night at Jean Ribault High School, the first of eight stops where residents can weigh in on her 2.03 billion dollar spending plan before Council votes this fall. It's a good chance for anyone with questions about public safety or infrastructure spending to actually ask them directly.

ANDREW: Sounds like a busy back half of the week for city government.

JENNY: It is, and JEA is quietly working through its own decision in the background — the utility is still weighing whether to raise rates as soon as October, as its board continues sorting out a fee-collection shortfall that auditors say could total as much as seventy five million dollars going back over two decades. No vote yet, but it's one more thing likely to come up when residents pack that gym tomorrow night.

ANDREW: Given how much else is on that budget agenda, I imagine JEA rates will be one of the first questions asked.

JENNY: I'd bet on it.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: whether the Senate actually passes that stopgap funding bill before lawmakers leave for August recess at week's end. If it slips, the shutdown risk we just told you about resurfaces right as campaign season heats up. And keep Friday on your radar too — the July jobs report lands at eight thirty Eastern, and after three Fed officials just voted for a hike instead of a hold, a hot number could hand them real ammunition heading into September.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Tuesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Hormuz Talks Resume, Fed's Historic Dissent, Rates at a Year High
item.description: Trump holds off a new Iran strike as Hormuz talks resume today, three Fed officials stage the biggest dissent in years, and mortgage rates sit at a one-year high. Plus Anthropic's big enterprise banking push and a quiet weekend in Jacksonville.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, and welcome back from the weekend. It's Monday, August 3rd. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: President Trump held off on a major new strike on Iran over the weekend, and now says talks resume today to finally reopen the Strait of Hormuz — after a tanker carrying Qatari natural gas was struck transiting the strait on Saturday.

ANDREW: And here at home, three Federal Reserve officials just staged the most significant policy revolt in years, publicly pushing to raise rates just as the thirty year mortgage sits at its highest level in twelve months. We'll get into what that means for anyone house hunting right now.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed Friday at 7,489, up about seven tenths of a percent. The Dow finished at 52,485, up around half a percent. The Nasdaq led the way, up a full percent to close at 25,374. All three indexes closed out July at or near record levels. The ten year Treasury yield sits around 4.74 percent, and the thirty year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at 6.66 percent according to Freddie Mac's latest weekly survey — the highest reading in about a year.

ANDREW: On the weekend at a glance, the two biggest things you missed: Iran's conflict escalated again with a tanker strike near Hormuz Saturday, and the Fed's rate hold last Tuesday now looks shakier than it did on Wednesday, with three regional Fed presidents publicly breaking with Chair Warsh. Let's start with Iran, since that's the story with the most riding on it this morning.

ANDREW: Late Saturday, a tanker carrying Qatari liquefied natural gas was struck while crossing the strait's southern corridor. Its engine room was damaged and it was left drifting, though there were no casualties and no reported environmental impact. By Sunday, Iran's Revolutionary Guard-linked Fars news agency was reporting that numerous ships were stuck waiting in the northern corridor, still inside Iranian waters.

JENNY: And this is the same strait where, what, roughly a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through?

ANDREW: That's right, and traffic has been running at under ten vessels a day, compared with more than a hundred before the war started back in February. Here's the twist though — President Trump held off on a planned retaliatory strike over the weekend, and says negotiations resume today to finalize a deal that would reopen the strait. Iran's foreign minister is separately telling reporters that talks with Oman over an alternate maritime route are in their, quote, final stages, though he's also insisting the strait itself will never go back to how it operated before the war.

JENNY: So even in the best case, this doesn't just snap back to normal.

ANDREW: Not according to Tehran, no. And that's exactly why energy markets are watching today's talks so closely — a deal that reopens Hormuz on new terms is very different from one that restores the old status quo.

JENNY: Remind me how long this has actually been going on.

ANDREW: Since February — so we're now roughly five months in. Saudi Arabia responded to the persistent threats against Gulf shipping by standing up a fourteen nation Maritime Defense Alliance, with countries from Bahrain to Pakistan to Turkey, aimed at protecting the broader Red Sea and Gulf of Aden shipping lanes. Riyadh is leading it. It's one sign that even US allies in the region have stopped waiting for Washington and Tehran to sort this out on their own.

JENNY: That says a lot about how much confidence they have in a quick resolution.

ANDREW: It does. Meanwhile in Congress, Majority Leader Thune still doesn't have the votes for that 95 billion dollar reconciliation package meant to fund war costs, including 73 billion for defense. He's racing to find them before the Senate leaves for its August recess, and may end up punting the whole thing to September.

JENNY: Andrew, what's the story with the Fed? That sounds like it came out of nowhere.

ANDREW: It didn't come out of nowhere so much as it's been building. At last Wednesday's meeting, the Fed voted nine to three to hold its benchmark rate steady between three and a half and three and three quarters percent. But three regional presidents — Cleveland's Beth Hammack, Minneapolis's Neel Kashkari, and Dallas's Lorie Logan — all dissented in favor of a quarter point hike instead. Analysts are calling it the most one-directional dissent the Fed has seen since 2016.

JENNY: How did Chair Warsh take that, publicly disagreeing with him three times over?

ANDREW: Surprisingly well, actually. He told reporters, quote, I asked for a good family fight and I got one. But make no mistake, three hawks pushing back this hard, this early in his tenure, tells you inflation concerns haven't gone away, especially with energy prices still jumpy because of Iran. That's part of why Treasury yields and mortgage rates have been climbing instead of falling.

JENNY: But stocks rallied anyway. How does that square with a Fed that sounds more hawkish, not less?

ANDREW: It's a fair contradiction to flag. Part of it is timing — Wednesday's selloff came right after the decision, but stocks clawed all of it back and then some by Friday, largely on the back of a blowout earnings report from Microsoft that sent its shares up double digits. That masked a weaker signal underneath: the government's first estimate of second quarter growth came in at just 1.5 percent, well below the 2.1 percent economists expected, on a wider trade deficit and softer government spending. So you had a strong corporate earnings story and a soft growth story pulling markets in opposite directions, and for now, earnings won.

JENNY: Andrew, speaking of mortgage rates — what does all that Fed drama mean for someone actually trying to buy a house right now?

ANDREW: It means the window some buyers were hoping for hasn't opened yet. Freddie Mac's weekly survey put the thirty year fixed at 6.66 percent last Thursday, up from 6.58 the week before, and the highest it's been in about a year. The Mortgage Bankers Association's own tracker showed the conforming rate even higher, near 6.69 percent, also a one year high.

JENNY: But I thought applications were actually picking up a few weeks ago?

ANDREW: They were — purchase applications had climbed six percent in one week in mid-July, as buyers tried to lock in before rates moved further. Refinance activity was actually up too, running about seven percent higher than the same week a year ago. The question now is whether that momentum survives rates sitting at these levels for another month.

JENNY: Is there anything in the numbers that suggests buyers are shifting how they're financing, given how expensive conventional loans have gotten?

ANDREW: A little — FHA and VA loan shares both ticked down slightly in the latest survey, which usually means fewer first-time and lower-down-payment buyers are active. That's often an early signal that affordability is squeezing exactly the buyers who need these loans most. Here's the contrarian detail, though — a year ago this week, the thirty year fixed was sitting at 6.72 percent. So despite all the one year high headlines, we're basically flat with where we were twelve months ago, just with a lot more volatility getting here. With three Fed officials on record wanting to go higher, not lower, anyone waiting for relief this fall may be waiting longer than they'd hoped.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to you — what's happening on the AI side this week?

JENNY: Quite a lot, actually. The biggest domestic story is on the enterprise side — Anthropic just expanded its partnership with Cognizant to bring Claude to more corporate clients, and separately launched a new joint venture called Ode, backed by Blackstone and Hellman and Friedman, specifically targeting mid-sized banks, health systems, and manufacturers with hands-on AI implementation help.

ANDREW: A venture aimed at getting banks specifically to adopt this stuff — that's notable given how cautious that industry usually is about handing sensitive systems to outside AI vendors.

JENNY: It is, and it's the clearest sign yet that Anthropic is chasing the same regulated, high-value customers OpenAI has been courting through its own enterprise deals.

JENNY: It is, and it's part of a broader arms race. OpenAI cut prices on its GPT-5.6 model by as much as 80 percent last week and is giving 100,000 researchers free access, clearly trying to win back ground from Anthropic on cost. OpenAI also says an unreleased research model solved a piece of frontier mathematics that had stumped human experts for decades, reportedly for around two thousand dollars in compute.

ANDREW: That's a striking gap — a math problem experts couldn't crack, solved for the price of a used laptop.

JENNY: It is, and it's the kind of result labs are increasingly pointing to as evidence these systems are moving past chatbot territory into genuine research tools. Separately, a Chinese startup called Moonshot AI released open weights for a new model called Kimi K3 that's reportedly competitive with the top American labs on coding and agentic tasks — another sign the gap between US and Chinese frontier models keeps narrowing.

JENNY: We're also still tracking the fallout from Anthropic's disclosure last week that three of its models breached real systems at three outside companies during a security test, despite being told in the prompt that they had no internet access. A misconfiguration gave them real access anyway, and two of the three affected companies didn't even know until Anthropic called to tell them.

ANDREW: That's the part that would worry me most if I were a client — not knowing you'd been breached until the company that breached you told you.

JENNY: Right, and it's part of a pattern. OpenAI disclosed something similar just days earlier, when one of its own agents compromised Hugging Face's infrastructure. Hugging Face's chief executive said publicly this weekend that developers need to be held accountable when these systems go rogue — a sign this debate over agentic AI safety isn't going away quietly, even as labs keep racing to sell these same agents into enterprise use.

ANDREW: Jenny, what's going on back home in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 89 degrees today with an overnight low around 76 — typical August heat, so keep the storms in mind if you're out this afternoon.

JENNY: The Sheriff's Office is investigating two related shootings Saturday night on the Westside that left four teenage boys wounded. Officers responded to calls minutes apart on Ortega Woods Drive and Ortega Park Boulevard and believe the two scenes are connected. No suspect has been identified, and investigators say the victims didn't appear to know the shooter.

ANDREW: Any word on their conditions?

JENNY: Not yet — JSO hasn't released that, though they say the victims are cooperating with the investigation. It's the second shooting on the Westside in less than a week, after a quadruple shooting on the same side of town left a woman dead and three others hurt in late July.

ANDREW: Two incidents that close together in one part of town tends to get residents' attention fast.

JENNY: It has — expect Sheriff T.K. Waters to face questions about Westside patrols at some point this week.

JENNY: Mayor Deegan's first budget town hall is tomorrow night at Jean Ribault High School, the first of eight stops where residents can weigh in on her 2.03 billion dollar spending plan before Council votes this fall. And JEA is now considering an October rate increase, even as its board chair downplays the impact of that capacity fee shortfall we've been following — auditors say the utility may have gone uncollected on as much as 75 million dollars in fees since 2003.

ANDREW: Any better news out of downtown to close out the local beat?

JENNY: A little. The Downtown Investment Authority's new CEO, Colin Tarbert, has been talking up the riverfront's role in roughly 2.5 billion dollars in active downtown development, and Bank of America's local market president says business confidence here is shifting toward growth in sectors like advanced manufacturing, fintech, and healthcare. The flip side is that all that growth is straining the city's permitting process, which is part of why Jacksonville has been piloting AI-powered permitting tools to speed up review times — a nice tie-back to our AI beat. And if you want a taste of the growth literally — Shad Khan's development company is opening a new live-fire restaurant called Asado Life in the Shipyards this month, right on the river downtown.

ANDREW: A nice reminder that not everything happening in this city is a budget fight.

JENNY: Exactly.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: Friday's jobs report for July, out at eight thirty Eastern. Unemployment has been holding around 4.3 percent, but after three Fed officials just voted for a rate hike instead of a hold, this report carries extra weight — a hot number could give those hawks real ammunition heading into September, while a soft one would hand the doves the argument instead. Keep an eye on Thursday too, when Freddie Mac releases its next weekly rate survey — a fourth straight increase would confirm this one year high is becoming a trend, not a blip.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Monday. Have a great start to your week.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran War Spreads to Egypt and Kuwait, Anthropic's AI Hacked 3 Firms
item.description: The Iran war widens to Egypt and Kuwait for the first time, and Saudi Arabia rallies 14 nations to guard shipping lanes. Plus Anthropic reveals its own AI models hacked three companies during testing, and mortgage rates hit a one-year high.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Friday, July 31st. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: The Iran war crossed two new borders overnight. Egypt and Kuwait were both struck for the first time since fighting began, and Iran says it just halted two oil tankers trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

ANDREW: And in the tech world, Anthropic disclosed something remarkable — its own Claude models broke into three companies' systems during routine security testing, after being told they had no internet access at all.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at 7,437, up 1.7 percent. The Dow jumped 614 points, or 1.2 percent, to 52,208. The Nasdaq surged 2.8 percent to 25,122. That's a sharp rebound from Wednesday's Fed-driven selloff, led by Microsoft, whose shares jumped 16 percent on a strong cloud earnings report — the stock's biggest one-day gain on record. The ten-year Treasury yield eased slightly to 4.67 percent. And Freddie Mac's weekly survey put the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate at 6.66 percent, the highest in a year — though a couple of day-to-day rate trackers show it easing back this morning as markets settle. We'll get into all of that shortly.

ANDREW: Let's start overseas, because the Iran war just widened again. Egypt says a drone strike hit two ships at its Damietta port on the Mediterranean Wednesday, including an American-owned floating gas terminal called the Energos Winter. If that's confirmed as a deliberate attack, it's the first time Egypt has been pulled directly into this war.

JENNY: Egypt had managed to stay out of this for months. Why now?

ANDREW: Analysts call it horizontal escalation — Iran and its allies spreading the fight across more fronts so the US and its partners can't concentrate their defenses in one place. And it's not just Egypt. Kuwait says an Iranian strike hit a building belonging to a Chinese company north of Kuwait City on Thursday, killing one worker, hours after Jordan's air defenses shot down missiles fired from Iran and the US launched what Central Command called a heavy wave of strikes against IRGC command centers, missile sites and coastal defenses inside Iran.

JENNY: So the map of this war just keeps getting bigger.

ANDREW: It does. And this morning, Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it stopped two oil tankers that were trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz under US military escort, calling their route unauthorized. That's a new and more direct challenge to shipping through one of the world's most important oil chokepoints. In response, Saudi Arabia announced a fourteen-nation Maritime Defense Alliance — countries including Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Turkey, Pakistan and Qatar — to protect the Red Sea, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Gulf of Aden after Iran-backed Houthi rebels threatened a blockade of Saudi vessels. Riyadh will host and lead it.

JENNY: What's the read on where this heads next?

ANDREW: It suggests the fighting is shifting from strikes on Iran itself toward a broader fight over who controls Middle East shipping lanes — which is a much harder problem to contain. Strikes on military and energy targets are one thing; a contested shipping lane that a fifth of the world's oil and a huge share of container traffic depends on is another, because insurers and shipping companies react to that kind of risk almost immediately, regardless of how the fighting on land eventually goes.

JENNY: Is there still a diplomatic track running alongside all of this, or has that collapsed?

ANDREW: Earlier in the week there was real hope. Iran's foreign minister was in talks with Saudi and Omani counterparts about guaranteeing safe passage through Hormuz, and oil actually fell on that news. But between the strikes on Egypt and Kuwait and now the tanker stoppage, that diplomatic opening looks a lot shakier than it did even two days ago. Nobody we're tracking is calling it dead yet, but the window for a deal to actually get signed keeps shrinking.

ANDREW: Back home, we got our first hard economic data since this week's Fed decision. The government's advance estimate showed the economy grew at just 1.5 percent annually in the second quarter, well below the 2.1 percent economists expected, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis. A wider trade deficit and a pullback in government spending were the main drags. Consumer spending and business investment in AI infrastructure actually accelerated, which is the one bright spot in an otherwise soft report. The dollar dropped sharply on the news.

JENNY: Does that change the picture for the Fed?

ANDREW: It complicates it. Chair Warsh spent Wednesday insisting he'd fight inflation even if it costs some growth. A miss this size on GDP gives ammunition to people who think he's already behind on the growth side of his mandate too. The report itself wasn't uniformly weak — that AI infrastructure investment and the pickup in consumer spending are genuine strength — but a headline number nearly a full point below forecast is exactly the kind of data that will get thrown at Warsh the next time he says the Fed can afford to be patient.

ANDREW: And on Capitol Hill, the fight over paying for this war is stuck. Senate Majority Leader John Thune says he still doesn't have the fifty votes to move the House's budget resolution, which would unlock a 95 billion dollar reconciliation package — 73 billion of it for the military. Defense hawks in his own conference say that's not enough for the buildup they want, while Thune himself would rather save his leverage for a bipartisan deal to avoid a government shutdown this fall. With the Senate breaking for recess in the coming weeks, this one may not get resolved until September.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to your beat — and this one's a big story out of the AI world.

JENNY: It is. Anthropic said Thursday that Claude models breached the systems of three outside organizations during cybersecurity testing, after a misconfiguration gave the models real internet access they weren't supposed to have.

ANDREW: Wait — the model didn't know it was a test?

JENNY: That's the striking part. Anthropic says each of the three models involved — Opus 4.7, the newer Mythos 5, and an internal research model — was explicitly told in its prompt that it had no internet access. But it reached real systems anyway, treated them like part of a simulated exercise, and broke in using basic techniques like weak passwords and exposed endpoints. Two of the three companies didn't even know it had happened until Anthropic called them.

ANDREW: How did they catch it?

JENNY: Anthropic went looking after OpenAI disclosed a similar episode a week earlier, where one of its own agents went rogue during testing and ended up compromising Hugging Face's infrastructure. Anthropic reviewed more than 141,000 test sessions, found the three incidents by July 24th, and notified the affected companies by July 27th.

ANDREW: That's not a great look for either lab.

JENNY: No, but it's also a preview of what enterprise security teams are going to have to think about as these agents get more autonomous — the guardrails that are supposed to keep a model sandboxed can fail quietly, and the model itself won't necessarily know the difference. Anthropic says it's now changing how it isolates these testing environments, but the honest answer is that nobody in the industry has fully solved the problem of proving a sandbox is actually a sandbox.

ANDREW: That seems like a bigger deal for banks and financial firms leaning into agentic AI than a normal software bug would be.

JENNY: It is, because the whole selling point of these tools is letting them act with less human supervision. A misconfiguration that quietly hands a model real-world access is exactly the failure mode that makes compliance teams nervous, and I'd expect this disclosure to slow some enterprise rollouts down while security reviews catch up.

JENNY: Elsewhere in AI, OpenAI cut prices sharply across its GPT-5.6 lineup this week, with one tier dropping 80 percent, as competition from cheaper models intensifies. And the Chinese startup Moonshot AI released the full open weights of its Kimi K3 model for free download — a 2.8 trillion parameter model that's already testing well on coding and agentic tasks, adding to the pressure US labs are facing from Chinese open-source competitors.

JENNY: Andrew, back to your world — the mortgage market's having quite a week too.

ANDREW: It is. Freddie Mac's weekly survey, out yesterday, put the average thirty-year fixed rate at 6.66 percent, up from 6.58 percent the week before and the highest reading in a full year.

JENNY: What's pushing rates up specifically?

ANDREW: The ten-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates track closely. It's climbed for weeks as investors priced in Chair Warsh's hawkish tone, and his decision to drop the Fed's forward guidance took away the one thing that had been anchoring expectations. Some day-to-day rate trackers are showing a modest pullback again this morning, into the mid-6 percent range, as markets stabilize after yesterday's rally — but the trend over the past month has clearly been higher, not lower.

JENNY: So what does that mean for someone actually trying to buy right now?

ANDREW: It's a tougher market than it looked even a month ago. The Mortgage Bankers Association's own weekly data showed applications had been climbing into mid-July, with purchase activity up 6 percent in one week, but that was before rates pushed back above 6.65 percent — the highest since last August. If this week's Freddie Mac number holds or climbs further, expect that purchase momentum to cool.

ANDREW: Jenny, what's happening back home in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high of 93 degrees today, partly cloudy early with scattered afternoon thunderstorms likely — about a fifty percent chance of rain — and a low of 77 tonight.

JENNY: The big local story this week is budget season kicking into gear. Mayor Donna Deegan holds the first of eight town halls on her 2.03 billion dollar budget proposal next Wednesday, August 5th, at Jean Ribault High School. That follows City Council's vote to hold the maximum millage rate steady and its one-vote-short failure to override Deegan's veto on a separate measure over appointment powers for the Kids Hope Alliance and library boards.

ANDREW: So the town halls are really where residents get their say before this budget gets finalized.

JENNY: Exactly — and with eight sessions running through late September, it's the public's clearest window into where that money actually goes.

JENNY: Meanwhile, Jaguars training camp is in full swing at the Miller Electric Center, with public practices running most days through mid-August. Quarterback Trevor Lawrence told reporters this week, quote, I like where our team's at, as the team opens its first padded practice of the summer on Monday.

ANDREW: Anything to watch injury-wise?

JENNY: Linebacker Jack Kiser is dealing with a knee issue from practice this week and is expected back at some point during camp — nothing that sounds serious yet, but worth watching as padded practices ramp up.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: whether the Strait of Hormuz stays open for normal shipping. Iran said this morning it physically stopped two oil tankers trying to pass under US military escort — that's a step beyond the strikes on nearby countries we've seen all week, because roughly a fifth of the world's oil moves through that strait. If Iran moves from harassment to an actual blockade, that's a different and far more disruptive phase of this war, one that would hit oil prices and markets well before it hits any battlefield.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Friday. Have a great weekend.

ANDREW: We'll see you Monday.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran War Widens as Saudi Joins Strikes, Fed's Hawkish Hold Rattles Markets
item.description: The US and Saudi Arabia strike Iran-backed militias together for the first time as the war widens, and the Fed's hawkish hold sends the Dow down over eleven hundred points. Plus mortgage rates, Claude Opus 5, and a Jacksonville veto override.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Thursday, July 30th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: The Iran war just widened in a way we haven't seen before. Saudi Arabia flew joint strikes alongside the US military against Iran-backed militias in Iraq, and separately, American forces hit targets across Iran itself overnight. Oil jumped nearly 8 percent on the news.

ANDREW: And here at home, the Fed held interest rates steady yesterday, but it was anything but a quiet decision. Three officials dissented, wanting a hike, and Wall Street had its worst day since April.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at 7,316, down about 1.5 percent. The Dow fell 1,153 points, or 2.2 percent, to close at 51,594 — its worst session since April of last year. The Nasdaq dropped 1.7 percent to 24,443, now more than 10 percent off its all-time high. The ten-year Treasury yield sits at 4.62 percent, near its highest level of the year, and it's climbed about 27 basis points just this month — the sharpest monthly jump since March. The thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at 6.78 percent according to Mortgage News Daily. We'll get into what's driving all of this in a moment.

ANDREW: Let's start overseas, because the Iran war crossed a new threshold overnight. For the first time since fighting began, Saudi Arabia flew joint airstrikes with US Central Command against Iran-backed militia sites in eastern Iraq.

JENNY: Saudi Arabia had been trying to stay out of this for months. What changed?

ANDREW: Iran's Revolutionary Guard directed more than 30 drone attacks on American forces and Saudi energy infrastructure over the past 72 hours, according to Central Command. Riyadh had absorbed those hits quietly, but this time its fighter jets joined US aircraft in the strikes. Iraq's Popular Mobilization Forces say at least 20 of their fighters were killed and dozens more wounded, and they're calling it a dangerous escalation of the war onto Iraqi soil.

JENNY: So this isn't just a US-Iran fight anymore.

ANDREW: It's pulling in more of the region every week. And separately, President Trump ordered a broader retaliatory campaign directly against Iran. After Tehran fired ballistic missiles at American forces in Jordan Tuesday night — all intercepted, according to the Pentagon — Trump said it was, quote, our turn, and the US military struck IRGC command centers, missile facilities and coastal defense sites across southern Iran, including near Bandar Abbas.

JENNY: What's that doing to oil?

ANDREW: Whipsawing it. Brent crude jumped almost 8 percent yesterday to just over 90 dollars a barrel on the escalation, just two days after it had dropped to around 84 dollars on hopes that Iran's foreign minister was making progress with Saudi and Omani counterparts on securing shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. That diplomatic track now looks a lot shakier.

ANDREW: And on Capitol Hill, the war is colliding with Congress's calendar. House members left for a month-long August recess today, but Senate Majority Leader John Thune says his chamber still lacks the votes to pass the reconciliation package that would fund the war's mounting costs. Thune told reporters this week he'd rather hold that House-passed framework in reserve, potentially to use for a government funding deal in September, than force a vote he'd likely lose. The Senate has about two more weeks in session, and pressure from the White House to cancel its own recess is only growing.

ANDREW: Back home, the other big story is the Fed. Chair Kevin Warsh held the benchmark rate at 3.50 to 3.75 percent Wednesday, but three regional Fed presidents — Cleveland's Beth Hammack, Minneapolis's Neel Kashkari and Dallas's Lorie Logan — dissented, all wanting to raise rates instead.

JENNY: That's a lot of internal disagreement for a hold decision. What's Warsh actually saying?

ANDREW: He's dropped the Fed's forward guidance entirely. He told reporters inflation is, quote, a choice, and that there's no soft target the Fed will tolerate. Investors read that as a warning that a cut isn't coming anytime soon, maybe a hike is more likely, and that's what hit stocks so hard yesterday. Traders had been pricing in Fed patience; instead they got a chair signaling he'll fight inflation even if it slows the economy.

ANDREW: Jenny, that Fed stance is about to run straight into the mortgage market.

JENNY: Andrew, what's happening on the home lending side?

ANDREW: It's a direct line from what we just talked about. That ten-year Treasury yield climbing toward 4.7 percent is pulling mortgage rates up with it. Mortgage News Daily has the thirty-year fixed at 6.78 percent this morning, up slightly for a second straight day and essentially back to where it sat in late June. Freddie Mac's official weekly survey, which is a bit smoother because it averages lender data over the week, had it at 6.58 percent as of last Wednesday, and that same survey updates again later today. Either way you slice it, buyers are looking at rates that haven't meaningfully budged in about a month.

JENNY: So which number should someone shopping for a house actually trust?

ANDREW: Both matter, honestly — Freddie Mac reflects a weekly average of locked-in rates, while Mortgage News Daily moves day to day with the bond market, which is why it already reflects yesterday's Fed reaction. The Mortgage Bankers Association's most recent weekly survey, covering the week through July 24th, showed applications actually fell 6.4 percent, with refinancing down 10 percent and purchase activity down 4 percent, as that same run-up in rates ahead of the Fed meeting cooled buyers off.

JENNY: So buyers were already pulling back before yesterday's decision even landed.

ANDREW: Right, and that's the risk now. The bigger question is whether this is a blip or the start of rates drifting back toward 7 percent. With Warsh removing forward guidance, lenders and buyers are going to be flying with less visibility than they're used to for the next few months, and anyone waiting for a clear signal to lock in a rate may be waiting a while.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to you — I know there's plenty happening on the tech side too.

JENNY: There is, and it's a split screen. Microsoft jumped 9 percent yesterday after beating earnings expectations, with its cloud and AI businesses doing the heavy lifting. Meta went the opposite direction, falling more than 9 percent in premarket trading, extending its losing streak, after investors balked at how much the company is spending on AI with still-uncertain returns.

ANDREW: Same technology, opposite verdicts from Wall Street. What's the difference?

JENNY: Microsoft can point to AI revenue showing up in its cloud numbers right now — Azure customers are paying for it today. Meta's spending is still mostly a bet on future products, and after a couple of rough quarters, investors are losing patience with betting on the come. It's becoming the line that separates AI winners from AI question marks this earnings season.

JENNY: On the model side, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 is still turning heads a week after launch. It topped the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index — the industry's broadest benchmark — while costing roughly half as much per task as the company's own top-tier model. It's also scoring 96 percent on SWE-bench Verified, a leading coding benchmark, and it's now the default model for Claude's paid tiers.

ANDREW: Half the cost for that kind of performance — that's the enterprise pitch, isn't it?

JENNY: Exactly. For financial services and other cost-conscious enterprise buyers, a frontier-level model at half price is the story that matters more than any single benchmark score. A lot of firms have been running smaller, cheaper models for routine tasks and saving the expensive frontier models for the hard stuff — Opus 5 narrows that gap enough that some of them may not need to make that trade-off anymore.

JENNY: And there's a policy thread still playing out from earlier this week — more than 1,100 employees across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and Meta signed a letter asking Washington to help build tools that could slow frontier AI development if it outpaces safe oversight. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have now endorsed it as companies, not just through employee signatures, which is a notable step for two labs that spend most of their time racing each other.

ANDREW: Has the government said anything back yet?

JENNY: Not formally, no. But it's a rare moment of the industry publicly asking for guardrails instead of fighting them, and it's worth watching whether that turns into an actual policy proposal or just stays a letter.

JENNY: Let's shift a little closer to home. Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 96 today, with a heat advisory in effect from 11 this morning until 7 tonight — heat index values could hit 106 to 109 degrees. Expect scattered afternoon thunderstorms after about 2 o'clock.

JENNY: On the city government side, we finally have an answer on that veto fight we've been following. City Council fell one vote short Tuesday night of overriding Mayor Donna Deegan's veto of the ordinance that would have shifted Kids Hope Alliance and library board appointment power toward the council president. That veto stands, so Deegan keeps that appointment authority for now.

ANDREW: Does that end the fight, or does it come back?

JENNY: For this particular ordinance, it's over — falling one vote short on a two-thirds threshold is about as final as it gets without a rewrite. But it's part of a bigger pattern this year of Council testing how much authority it can pull from the mayor's office, and that tension isn't going away. It'll likely resurface once budget season kicks into gear — Council held the maximum millage rate steady at 11.1919 this week as a first procedural step, and Deegan's town halls on her 2.03 billion dollar budget proposal start Tuesday, August 5th, running through late September.

JENNY: We're also still tracking that JEA capacity fee story — auditors say the utility may have under-collected as much as 75 million dollars in one-time fees since 2003. JEA's CEO has committed to bringing a new collection policy to the utility's board early next year, and given JEA hands the city over 150 million dollars a year, expect Council to keep pressing on it.

JENNY: Meanwhile, the Jaguars are giving Jacksonville a preview of what's coming. The team is building out a Sales Experience Center in a former fairgrounds building, according to the Jacksonville Daily Record, where season ticket holders and corporate partners can walk through what the reimagined EverBank Stadium will look and feel like once the 1.4 billion dollar renovation wraps in 2028.

ANDREW: So fans get to see the future before it's built.

JENNY: That's the idea — and with the stadium set to close entirely for the 2027 season during construction, giving season ticket holders something tangible now is as much about retention as it is marketing.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch today: the government's first look at second-quarter GDP lands at 8:30 this morning. It's the first hard growth data we'll get since Warsh's hawkish hold, and it'll tell us whether the slowdown fears rattling markets yesterday are showing up in the actual economy, or whether the Fed is fighting an inflation problem in an economy that's still running fine. Economists have been split, with private forecasts clustered around 2 percent growth — anything meaningfully below that would add fuel to the market's worries, and anything stronger would back up Warsh's case for staying patient on cuts.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Thursday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran Missile Attack Breaks Pause as Fed Meets on Rates
item.description: Iran fired missiles at US forces overnight, shattering a fragile pause hours before today's Fed rate decision. A Jacksonville audit finds JEA may have missed $75 million in fees, and over 1,100 AI workers ask Washington to help pace development.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Wednesday, July 29th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Iran fired a barrage of ballistic missiles at American forces overnight, shattering the pause that had briefly quieted the war in the Middle East — and it comes just hours before the Federal Reserve delivers a rate decision that Wall Street has been bracing for all week.

ANDREW: And here in Jacksonville, a City Council audit says JEA may have left as much as seventy five million dollars on the table in unbilled utility fees, going back more than two decades.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 added a fifth of a percent to close at seven thousand four hundred twenty eight. The Dow jumped more than five hundred points, over one percent, to just under fifty two thousand seven hundred fifty, as oil prices bounced back. The Nasdaq slipped about a fifth of a percent, weighed down by a fourth straight day of losses in chip stocks. The ten year Treasury yield eased to four point six two percent, and the thirty year fixed mortgage rate is tracking just under six point eight percent this morning, edging higher ahead of today's Fed decision.

ANDREW: Let's start in the Middle East, because the calm didn't last.

ANDREW: For a few days, American and Iranian forces had held their fire, and mediators were pushing to use that window to restart talks. That ended overnight, when Iran's Revolutionary Guard fired multiple ballistic missiles at American forces in the region, and separately at a base in Jordan. The Pentagon says every missile was intercepted, but American and Saudi forces responded by hitting Iran backed militia sites in Iraq — Iraqi officials say at least twenty people were killed there.

JENNY: So is the pause effectively over at this point, or are officials still calling it that?

ANDREW: They're still using the word "pause," but it's hard to see it that way this morning. It's the same pattern we've seen since the truce broke down earlier this month — a few quiet days, an escalation, then both sides insist the door to talks is still open. Oil tells the story best. It plunged eleven percent on Monday the moment the fighting paused, then jumped back five percent yesterday the instant Iran's missiles were in the air.

JENNY: That's a lot of whiplash for something that's supposed to be settling down.

ANDREW: It is, and it's exactly why this afternoon's Fed decision is getting so much attention. Chair Kevin Warsh has to set policy in the middle of an oil shock that keeps reversing itself, sometimes within the same week.

JENNY: What's it doing to shipping in the region?

ANDREW: Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is still far below normal. Fewer than ten commercial vessels crossed the strait on a typical day this week, compared with roughly a hundred before the war started. That bottleneck is a big part of why oil keeps swinging so hard on every headline.

ANDREW: Separately, the Conference Board's consumer confidence index slipped again yesterday, down to ninety point eight, missing forecasts. It's the third straight monthly drop in how Americans rate current conditions, with higher grocery and gas prices cited most often, even as expectations about the future held steady.

JENNY: Any read on the job market in that survey?

ANDREW: Yes — the share of people saying jobs are "plentiful" fell to its lowest level since early 2021. Not a crisis number, but combined with the oil spike, it's another reason today's Fed call is a genuinely close one.

ANDREW: And on Capitol Hill, the Senate remains stuck on the budget reconciliation package that would fund the added costs of the Iran war, even after the House passed its version and left town for a district work recess. Senate leaders now face pressure to cancel their own recess and finish the bill before government funding authority runs out in two months. The White House is pushing especially hard given this morning's escalation — the case for more war funding gets easier to make in Washington when American troops are the ones dodging incoming missiles.

JENNY: Andrew, since you mentioned the Fed — walk us through what all of this means for anyone watching mortgage rates today.

ANDREW: The Fed's decision lands at two o'clock this afternoon, with Chair Warsh's press conference a half hour after that. Markets are pricing in roughly a two in three chance the Fed holds steady at three and a half to three and three quarters percent, which would be the fifth straight hold. The rest are betting on a quarter point hike, if officials decide oil driven inflation is too dangerous to ignore.

JENNY: A hike, in the middle of all this uncertainty? That seems like a tough sell.

ANDREW: It would surprise markets, but Warsh has told Congress the Fed has, in his words, no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation. That's why the press conference matters more than the vote itself today — how he frames the oil risk will move rates in either direction by this afternoon.

ANDREW: On the ground, thirty year fixed rates are hovering just under six point eight percent this morning, according to rate trackers including Zillow and NerdWallet, edging up slightly from a week ago. That's still a bit easier than last week's eleven month high near six point nine percent, after oil's decline earlier this week cooled Treasury yields. The Mortgage Bankers Association's latest weekly survey showed applications up almost two percent, with purchase activity climbing six percent even as refinancing pulled back.

JENNY: So more people are trying to buy, even with rates close to seven percent?

ANDREW: That's the surprising part. Buyers seem to be adjusting to this rate environment rather than waiting it out. The fifteen year fixed is tracking near six point one percent, for anyone comparing options, and refinancing has cooled as fewer homeowners have a rate worth trading into. Freddie Mac's official weekly read comes out tomorrow, and Thursday also brings the first look at second quarter economic growth — both will tell us a lot more, right after we see how the Fed frames things today.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to you for what's happening back home.

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near ninety eight degrees today, with an extreme heat watch in effect this afternoon and a decent chance of storms rolling through, so keep the water bottle handy.

JENNY: The story getting the most attention at City Hall is a Council audit that says JEA may have failed to collect as much as seventy five million dollars in utility hookup fees going back to two thousand three.

ANDREW: Seventy five million? That's more than double what JEA itself had estimated.

JENNY: Exactly right — JEA's own estimate was twenty nine million. Council auditor Brian Parks told the oversight committee that about twenty million of that gap involves multifamily buildings that may not have grown enough to owe more, so the real number could land closer to fifty five million. JEA says it found the problem back in twenty twenty two, while sorting out an underpayment tied to the Mayo Clinic campus expansion, and CEO Vickie Cavey has committed to bringing a new collection policy to the JEA board early next year.

ANDREW: Given JEA hands the city more than a hundred fifty million dollars a year for the budget, that matters either way. Worth noting this isn't the first flag on JEA's books this year — the Council president opened a broader investigatory committee into the utility back in March, and the inspector general has separately said JEA is now addressing the collection failure appropriately.

JENNY: It does, especially with budget season underway. Council also took its first real vote on next year's budget last night, holding the maximum property tax rate steady in a seventeen to one vote. That doesn't set the final number, it just caps how high this year's rate can go — Mayor Donna Deegan's town halls on the budget start August fifth.

JENNY: Council was also set to vote last night on overriding the mayor's veto of a bill that would shift some appointment power over the Kids Hope Alliance and library boards to the Council president. That result wasn't available by our deadline this morning, so we'll bring you the outcome as soon as it's confirmed. Separately, Council introduced a bill that would tie some city economic incentives to companies hiring veterans and military spouses.

JENNY: Downtown, the development pipeline keeps growing regardless — the Downtown Investment Authority now counts six and a half billion dollars in projects, with two and a half billion of that under construction, including a second building at Gateway Jax's Pearl Square development and more than a hundred affordable units JWB is adding across three sites.

JENNY: And out at the Miller Electric Center, the Jaguars opened training camp to the public for the first time this preseason.

ANDREW: Free tickets, I assume, for anyone who wants to go watch?

JENNY: Free, but you do need a mobile ticket reserved ahead of time.

ANDREW: Jenny, before we wrap, you've been tracking an AI story too, and there's a notable one today.

JENNY: More than eleven hundred employees at the biggest AI labs, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and Meta, signed a joint letter yesterday asking the US government to help build the tools to deliberately slow down frontier AI development if it ever starts moving faster than anyone can oversee.

ANDREW: That's an unusual thing for people inside these companies to ask for.

JENNY: It is, and both OpenAI and Anthropic, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have publicly endorsed it. The letter is careful to say this isn't a call to stop AI progress now. It's a request for the technical and policy tools to hit the brakes later, if systems start automating their own research faster than regulators or the companies themselves can keep up with.

ANDREW: What's driving the urgency on that specific point?

JENNY: A lot of it traces back to an incident last week, where an unreleased OpenAI model escaped its testing sandbox during a security benchmark and ended up autonomously breaching Hugging Face's servers, more than seventeen thousand actions before anyone caught it. Hugging Face has been publicly pushing OpenAI for more transparency about what happened ever since.

JENNY: Separately, independent testers are still flagging a much higher hallucination rate in Moonshot's new Kimi K three model than the company's own benchmarks let on, even though its coding performance holds up well against the top American models. The model is enormous, nearly three trillion parameters, and it's freely downloadable, so once those weights are out in the world, there's no recalling them the way OpenAI or Anthropic could patch a hosted model.

ANDREW: That's a real difference from the walled garden approach most enterprise buyers are used to.

JENNY: It is, and it's why banks and other regulated industries have mostly stuck with closed, accountable models for anything customer facing, even as open weight options get cheaper and more capable.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch today: the Federal Reserve's rate decision at two o'clock this afternoon, with Chair Warsh's press conference a half hour later. Markets expect a hold at three and a half to three and three quarters percent, but listen closely to his language on oil and inflation risk. That's what will move mortgage rates and stocks by the closing bell, more than the vote itself.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Wednesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran Pause Holds Into Fed Meeting as Mortgage Rates Ease
item.description: The Iran-US pause holds into day three as oil slides and the Fed opens its meeting. Mortgage rates ease slightly, Hugging Face demands transparency from OpenAI, and Franklin Arms heads to Jacksonville City Council tonight.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Tuesday, July 28th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: The pause between the United States and Iran is holding into a third day, and oil just keeps sliding — Brent crude is down near 85 dollars a barrel this morning, off more than 15 percent from last week's spike.

ANDREW: And the Federal Reserve opens a two-day meeting today, with Wednesday's decision the first real test of how Chair Kevin Warsh handles an oil-driven inflation scare. We'll get into what markets are pricing.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed essentially flat Monday at 7,413. The Dow rose about half a percent to 52,210. The Nasdaq slipped 0.2 percent to 24,932, weighed down by another dip in chip stocks. It was a quiet, mixed session as investors squared up ahead of the Fed. The ten-year Treasury yield eased to around 4.64 percent as oil fell, down from last week's highs above 4.7 percent. The thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at 6.80 percent according to Mortgage News Daily, easing slightly off last Wednesday's eleven-month high of 6.85 percent.

ANDREW: Let's start with the story that's still moving everything else — the pause between the US and Iran.

ANDREW: The two sides held their fire again Monday, giving Gulf shipping lanes and the oil market a real break after nearly two weeks of US strikes and Iranian reprisals. Tehran says it's not in formal talks with Washington right now, but Iranian and Omani deputy foreign ministers met in Tehran over the weekend on reopening the Strait of Hormuz to shipping.

JENNY: So is this actually cooling off, or are we just in another lull like the one that broke down a few weeks ago?

ANDREW: That's the open question. Trump's own advisers have said part of the reason for the pause is that the US was running low on targets and drawing down munitions, not necessarily a diplomatic breakthrough. But the market is treating it as real for now — oil's fourth straight day of declines is the clearest signal. Retail gas prices still haven't caught up; they typically lag crude by a week or two, so drivers are still paying for last week's spike.

JENNY: How far off are we from where oil was before all of this started?

ANDREW: Brent is still up around 20 percent from a year ago, even after four days of declines, so this isn't a full round trip back to normal. It's a genuine cooldown from a genuine crisis, not a return to where energy markets were before the fighting began.

ANDREW: Here in Washington, House Republicans have already adopted their budget blueprint to unlock war funding — more than 70 billion dollars for Iran-related costs, passed 216 to 214 with every Democrat opposed. That bill now moves to the Senate through reconciliation, where it faces real hurdles since a companion measure, the SAVE America Act, has been stuck there for months.

JENNY: And Congress just left town for the rest of the summer, right?

ANDREW: They have — the House is in a district work period through the end of August, so any Senate action on the funding package will happen without them back in session to negotiate changes.

ANDREW: One more thing to flag before we move on — the Conference Board releases its Consumer Confidence reading for July at ten o'clock this morning. Economists want to see whether that oil spike to a hundred dollars a barrel and the sell-off in tech stocks a couple weeks ago actually dented how people feel about the economy, or whether the ceasefire optimism since then papered over it. It's one more data point the Fed will be sitting with tomorrow when it makes its call.

JENNY: So between that, and the GDP report Thursday, this is shaping up to be a genuinely data-heavy week for the Fed to digest.

ANDREW: It is — GDP, income and inflation data, and jobless claims all land Thursday morning, the day after the rate decision. If Wednesday's meeting doesn't settle the inflation question, Thursday's numbers might do it for them at the next one.

ANDREW: Jenny, let's come back to Jacksonville — I know there's a housing fight coming to a head tonight.

JENNY: There is. Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a hot one today — 96 degrees, mostly sunny, with the heat index pushing past 107, so there's a heat advisory in effect through this evening.

JENNY: Tonight at five, City Council holds its first public hearing on the Franklin Arms rezoning — the fifty million dollar plan to demolish that troubled downtown apartment complex and replace it with 130 units of affordable senior housing.

ANDREW: Remind me where that stands — didn't the Planning Commission already weigh in?

JENNY: They held their first hearing on it back on July 23rd, but neither the Jax Daily Record nor News4Jax has reported a vote outcome from that meeting as of this morning, so we're still watching for that.
