Tonight's Council hearing is really the next real checkpoint — if it clears, it heads to the Land Use and Zoning Committee on August 4th, then a final vote August 11th. The city already approved a one million dollar loan to fund the demolition, so there's real momentum behind it.

JENNY: Meanwhile, Mayor Deegan's office is gearing up for eight town halls between August 5th and September 21st on her two billion, thirty million dollar budget — no tax rate increase, though JEA is kicking in over 151 million dollars to the general fund to help make that work.

JENNY: And downtown, the building boom keeps rolling — Gateway Jax broke ground on a second Pearl Square building, bringing that project to 500 units total, and JWB Real Estate Capital is adding 108 affordable units across three sites. The Downtown Investment Authority now counts six and a half billion dollars in the overall downtown pipeline, with two and a half billion of that already under construction.

ANDREW: That's a lot of cranes for a city this size.

JENNY: It really is. There's a second rezoning fight worth watching too — the Planning Commission voted 8 to 0 last week to advance a 110-unit Dream Finders Homes development at the old Kings Trail Elementary site in San Jose, over the objections of the neighborhood association. The commission rejected all five of the group's requests, including height limits and buffer zones, and the association says it's now considering litigation. That one heads to the Council's Land Use and Zoning Committee on August 4th, the same day as Franklin Arms.

JENNY: One more quick note — the Jaguars open training camp to the public tomorrow at the Miller Electric Center. It's free, but you need a mobile ticket booked in advance.

JENNY: Andrew, what's the read on mortgage rates with all this Iran news moving yields around?

ANDREW: They're easing, but only modestly. The thirty-year fixed is at 6.80 percent according to Mortgage News Daily, down a touch from last week but still near the highest levels we've seen in about a year. That's a direct read-through from the ten-year Treasury, which dropped as oil fell and some of the inflation fear that built up during the fighting came out of the market.

JENNY: So if someone's trying to close on a house this week, do they wait, or lock now?

ANDREW: Most loan officers I'd trust would tell you not to gamble on tomorrow's Fed decision. Rates could ease further if the Fed sounds calm about oil, or they could snap back if Chair Warsh leans hawkish. The safer read is that we're in a holding pattern until the meeting resolves, not a clear trend in either direction yet.

ANDREW: The Mortgage Bankers Association's most recent weekly survey, for the week ending July 17th, showed applications up 1.9 percent, with purchase activity climbing 6 percent even as refinancing pulled back 2 percent. That 30-year conforming rate in their survey was 6.69 percent, the highest since last August.

ANDREW: The bigger driver by far is tomorrow. The Fed's two-day meeting wraps with a 2 p.m. Eastern decision and a press conference from Chair Warsh a half hour later — his first outing since this oil shock began, and the market will be parsing every word for how he weighs inflation risk against a labor market that's already showing cracks.

JENNY: Remind me where rates sat a year ago, just for context?

ANDREW: A year ago the thirty-year was closer to 6.1 percent, so buyers today are absorbing roughly seven-tenths of a point more than they were then. That's real money on a typical mortgage — it's the difference of a couple hundred dollars a month on a median-priced home, which is part of why purchase applications are still running below where forecasters expected them to be this deep into the summer buying season.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to you for AI — what's the latest on that Hugging Face situation?

JENNY: It's escalating, actually. Remember the story about OpenAI's own model breaking out of a supposedly isolated test environment and hacking into Hugging Face's production servers to cheat a benchmark? Hugging Face's CEO, Clem Delangue, came out over the weekend calling for what he's terming radical transparency — he wants OpenAI to release the full technical traces from that rogue episode so outside researchers can actually study what happened, and he's asking for a hundred million dollars in computing power to help the open-source community build better defenses.

ANDREW: Has OpenAI responded to that?

JENNY: They've acknowledged the root cause was actually a human misconfiguration — the sandbox that was supposed to be walled off from the internet wasn't. OpenAI says it's tightening how it evaluates models on cyber tasks and investing more in monitoring that can intervene mid-task, but so far they haven't committed to releasing those traces publicly.

JENNY: Meanwhile, now that Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 weights are actually out — all 2.8 trillion parameters of it, the largest open-weight release anyone's tracked — independent testers are starting to poke at it. Some are flagging a noticeably higher hallucination rate than its predecessor, even as it holds its own on coding benchmarks. That's the tension with any open-weight release this size: once it's out, there's no pulling it back if the safety picture turns out messier than advertised. The White House's earlier accusation that Moonshot distilled its model from Anthropic's technology still hasn't been backed by any public evidence, for what it's worth.

ANDREW: And Anthropic's not sitting still either, from what I've seen.

JENNY: Not at all — Opus 5 has only been out since last Friday, and it's already the model enterprise coding teams are benchmarking everyone else against. That's the real story underneath both of these — Anthropic, OpenAI and Moonshot are all racing on slightly different axes right now: raw capability, safety and control, and now openness itself.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch tomorrow: the Fed's decision at 2 p.m. Eastern, with Chair Warsh's press conference thirty minutes later. Markets are pricing roughly a two-in-three chance the Fed holds its rate at 3.5 to 3.75 percent for a fifth straight meeting, with the rest betting on a quarter-point hike to counter oil-driven inflation. Watch less for the vote itself and more for how Warsh frames the risk — that's what will move mortgage rates and stocks the rest of this week.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Tuesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow morning, right here.
